summary: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality, yet the real-world performance of FDA-cleared AI detection models remains incompletely characterized. We retrospectively evaluated two FDA-cleared AI algorithms from a single commercial platform (Aidoc Medical BriefCase)—one for PE triage on dedicated CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA; n = 30,678) and one for incidental PE (iPE) detection on routine contrast-enhanced CTs (n = 37,191), across a 17-facility academic health system. Reference-standard labels were extracted from radiology reports using a validated LLM pipeline (97% accuracy, κ = 0.94). The PE model achieved 86.8% sensitivity and 99.1% specificity, with sensitivity declining from 99.3% for saddle emboli to 72.9% for subsegmental PE, and from 89.7% for acute to 65.3% for non-acute PE. The iPE model achieved 73.5% sensitivity and 99.8% specificity. Both models demonstrated lower sensitivity than FDA-clearance benchmarks while exceeding cleared specificity, with diminishing performance for peripheral and non-acute emboli mirroring known human reader limitations and underscoring the need for standardized post-market surveillance of AI-enabled medical devices.

summary: Evaluation of AI-generated patient communication lacks standardized frameworks, and automated metrics may not reflect clinical utility. We leveraged a staged rollout of GPT-generated draft responses (GDRs) to patient portal messages. Thirty primary care physicians received drafts from September 2023 to August 2024 under two conditions: an intervention group where AI drafts were displayed and edited (n = 21,073), and a non-displayed group where drafts were generated but never shown to physicians, who composed responses independently (n = 45,127). We evaluated messages using BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, and Flesch Reading Ease, and then correlated automated metrics with blinded physician ratings of effectiveness, misunderstanding potential, and harm. In the intervention group, 2264 (11%) drafts were incorporated into final messages with high semantic alignment (BERTScore F1 = 0.93). In the non-displayed group, independent physician messages showed moderate similarity to unseen drafts (BERTScore F1 = 0.83). Despite comparable semantic scores, physicians preferred human-authored messages (4.24/5). BERTScore correlated with physician quality ratings in the intervention group but not in the non-displayed. Automated metrics demonstrated context-dependent validity; they assessed editing fidelity but failed to evaluate whether AI-generated content matches independent human performance. Rigorous evaluation of clinical generative AI requires validation of metric meaning within specific use contexts.

summary: Despite long-standing immunization programs, pertussis remains a major cause of vaccine-preventable mortality, particularly among infants. Here we present a primary assessment of global pertussis incidence, mortality and disability-adjusted life years across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. We show that despite short-term pandemic-period fluctuations, the dominant global pattern from 1990 to 2023 was long-term decline: age-standardized mortality decreased by 61.2% and age-standardized incidence by 41.6%. Relative to the anomalously low pandemic-period estimates, incidence and mortality rebounded by 102.6% (95% uncertainty interval, 77.0–128.2%) and 66.1% (95% uncertainty interval, 2.4–174.5%), respectively, between 2020 and 2023. In 2023 alone, we estimated 18.9 million cases and 115,000 deaths attributable to pertussis. This burden remains profoundly inequitable and inversely correlated with the sociodemographic index; sub-Saharan Africa now accounts for roughly 65% of global deaths, with the highest population-adjusted risk concentrated among infants younger than 6 months. Our findings highlight a modeled geographic concentration of pertussis mortality and support strengthening timely infant vaccination, maternal immunization where recommended and feasible and robust surveillance in highly susceptible regions. Updates to the Global Burden of Disease study showed that while global trends in pertussis (whooping cough) declined from 1990 to 2023, the rebound in incidence and mortality since 2020, particularly in high-income regions, reflects stalled vaccination progress worldwide.
title: Global, regional and national burden of pertussis in 1990–2023: a Global Burden of Disease study

summary: Radiotherapy (RT) remains a cornerstone in managing lower-grade glioma (LGG), but its response varies widely. Reliable pre-treatment prediction of RT response could facilitate patient management but remains unavailable. Here we present GUARD-LGG, a machine learning model designed to predict early RT response in LGG before treatment. GUARD-LGG was trained on 963 patients from a major center, tested on 187 patients from seven independent institutions, and 328 patients prospectively enrolled in a registered clinical trial. GUARD-LGG achieved AUCs of 0.946 (95% CI: 0.938–0.962), 0.929 (95% CI: 0.894–0.965), 0.882 (95% CI: 0.830–0.934), and 0.913 (95% CI: 0.878–0.949) in the training, internal validation, external, and prospective test sets, respectively. Model interpretation highlighted residual tumor, age, T2-weighted texture roughness and T1-weighted contrast intensity changes as major predictors. Radiogenomic analyses suggested potential associations between predicted unfavorable RT response and enrichment of RT resistance-related pathways. Consistently, patients with predicted unfavorable RT response exhibited shorter overall survival. In conclusion, GUARD-LGG enables individualized prediction of early RT response before therapy, offering a tool for pre-treatment response stratification in LGG.
title: GUARD-LGG: a glioma upfront AI-driven radiotherapy response decipher for lower-grade glioma

summary:
Background

Medicare Advantage insurers conduct in-home health risk assessments (HRAs) to identify high-risk patients and facilitate appropriate care. Critics argue this practice increases risk-adjusted payments without improving quality. Comprehensive data on use of in-home HRAs and downstream treatment are lacking.

Objective

To examine trends in cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during in-home HRAs, characteristics associated with HRA-based diagnoses, and treatment rates after diagnoses.

Design

Cohort study.

Setting

Population-based.

Participants

Medicare Advantage beneficiaries.

Measurements

Using 100% Medicare claims, trends in the proportion of cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during in-home HRAs (vs. facility-based visits) were examined. Multivariable logistic regression models were fit to estimate the association between beneficiary- and plan-level characteristics and HRA-based diagnoses and compare treatment rates across settings.

Results

Among 21 496 506 Medicare Advantage beneficiaries diagnosed with a cardiovascular risk factor or disease, the proportion diagnosed during in-home HRAs increased between 2018 and 2022 for hypertension (45.9% to 47.7%), hyperlipidemia (57.8% to 66.7%), diabetes (47.8% to 51.6%), atrial fibrillation (30.0% to 36.0%), ischemic heart disease (37.2% to 41.6%), peripheral vascular disease (64.5% to 73.9%), and heart failure (34.7% to 42.6%). Racial and ethnic minority beneficiaries and those enrolled in lower-rated plans were more likely to receive HRA-based diagnoses. Treatment rates were substantially lower after HRA-based diagnoses across all conditions.

Limitations

Differences in the severity of conditions between groups could not be assessed. Prescription fills were used as a proxy for management. Observed differences in the diagnosis and treatment of conditions across encounter settings may be susceptible to unmeasured confounding.

Conclusion

Among Medicare Advantage beneficiaries, an increasingly large share of cardiovascular conditions are being diagnosed through in-home HRAs, but treatment rates after these diagnoses are consistently lower than after facility-based encounters.

Primary funding source

National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Cardiovascular Conditions in Medicare Advantage In-Home Health Risk Assessments.

summary:
Background

The United States recently proposed changes to the recommendations for childhood hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination.

Objective

To project the effect of vaccine policy changes, if fully implemented, on chronic HBV infections.

Design

Markov cohort state transition model of perinatal and childhood HBV infection.

Data sources

Published data on maternal HBV prevalence (0.4%) and hepatitis B surface antigen testing (99.5% sensitivity), childhood vaccine completion (universal birth-dose strategy: 91.1%; deferred strategy: 87.1%; shared decision-making strategy: 50.0%), and age-stratified risk for chronic HBV infection.

Target population

One-year birth cohort of U.S.-born infants (n = 3.6 million).

Time horizon

20 years.

Intervention

Universal birth-dose vaccination, deferred (2-month) vaccination, and vaccination through shared decision making.

Outcome measures

Numbers with chronic HBV infection and susceptibility to HBV, with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs) derived from probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

Results of base-case analysis

Compared with the universal birth-dose strategy (255 childhood infections [95% UI, 130 to 530]), the deferred and shared decision-making strategies would increase chronic HBV infections in the 2026 birth cohort by 19% to 303 (95% UI, 155 to 610) and by 83% to 467 (95% UI, 209 to 1032), respectively. These strategies would also increase the number of HBV-susceptible people at year 20 (474 000 and 1 806 000) compared with the universal birth-dose strategy (232 000).

Results of sensitivity analysis

In a scenario with lower vaccine coverage (84.5%) and higher HBV prevalence (maternal prevalence of 0.72% and higher risk for horizontal infection), chronic HBV infections would increase to 1700 and 2192, respectively, with the deferred and shared decision-making strategies.

Limitation

Uncertainty in horizontal HBV infection risk.

Conclusion

Proposed policy changes for vaccination through shared decision making are projected to result in an 83% increase in childhood HBV infections, and between 50% and 70% of children entering adulthood annually would be susceptible to HBV infection. Policymakers should reimplement recommendations for universal birth-dose vaccination.

Primary funding source

National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.
title: Projected Effect of 2026 Federal Changes to the Childhood Immunization Schedule on Chronic Hepatitis B Virus Infections in the United States.

summary: The opioid use disorder (OUD) epidemic in the United States has been a major public health crisis. We developed OUD-REY (OUD Risk Evaluator at 1 Year) - a deep learning model that uses longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data from the All of Us research program to predict risk of OUD at one year for patients with an opioid prescription. On internal validation, OUD-REY achieved an AUROC of 91.2% and AUPRC of 77.0%. We leveraged a pretrained language model to accommodate thousands of unseen, out-of-vocabulary clinical features in a patient’s longitudinal EHR history. We externally validated our model on a new dataset released by All of Us that was temporally separated from our development set and on a dataset containing ~6 million patients from medical centers of the Veterans Affairs (VA) nationwide over a span of 20 years. On external validation, our model had an AUROC and AUPRC of 86.4% and 23.1% (OUD prevalence of 2.9%), respectively, on our temporally separated All of Us validation set. It had an AUROC and AUPRC of 85.5% and 19.5% (OUD prevalence of 3.5%), respectively, on the VA dataset. Our fairness auditing showed that the model was generally fair for patients with different genders, race, and ethnic backgrounds. This model may potentially improve prevention and care of OUD.

Postinduction MRD-negativity rates varied significantly across gene expression subtypes, with HP1/HP3 and MS groups showing superior responses compared to the MF and CD2 subtypes. B cell differentiation was associated with MRD positivity, while proliferation and MYC programs were associated with MRD negativity. These MRD-associated transcriptomic features were independently validated in the CASSIOPEIA cohort. Whole-genome sequencing revealed both known (APOBEC mutagenesis, chromothripsis) and new genomic instability phenotypes validated in the MMRF cohort. New driver alterations were identified with independent validation across three external cohorts with multiple myeloma (MMRF, MANHATTAN and CASSIOPEIA; 1,451 cases). Genomic instability features and driver genes such as CCND1 and MYC correlated with differential MRD outcomes. DNA methylation profiling identified nine MRD-linked subgroups distinguished by the extent of hypomethylation in quiescent chromatin and cis/trans signatures of driver translocations. A multimodal random forest model integrating genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic features predicted MRD status after induction, with an area under the curve of 0.77, outperforming clinical and genomic models, while providing comparable discrimination and improved calibration relative to the transcriptomic and epigenomic models. These findings define a multiomic classification of NDMM linked to Isa-KRd response. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04934475 . In a multiomic analysis of samples from patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma treated with isatuximab, carfilzomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone induction therapy followed by consolidation treatment guided by minimal residual disease (MRD) status, baseline genomic, transcriptomic and epigenetic features are associated with MRD status after induction.

summary:
Importance

It remains unclear if intraoperative hemodynamic therapy should be guided by cardiac index.

Objective

To evaluate whether individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy vs routine hemodynamic therapy improves outcomes in high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery.

Design, setting, and participants

This multicenter, single-blind, superiority randomized clinical trial enrolled high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery between October 8, 2023, and October 25, 2025, at 12 university medical centers in Austria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, and Spain. The date of last follow-up was January 15, 2026.

Interventions

Patients were randomized to individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy targeting the patient's preoperative resting cardiac index vs routine hemodynamic therapy (with blinded cardiac index monitoring).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was a composite of acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within the first 7 postoperative days. Secondary outcomes included the individual components of the primary outcome within the first 7 postoperative days.

Results

Of the 1128 patients enrolled, 1111 were randomized and 1095 were included in the primary analysis (median age, 67 years [IQR, 59-74 years]; 49.4% were female). The primary outcome occurred in 243 of 549 patients (44.3%) in the individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy group vs 256 of 546 patients (46.9%) in the routine hemodynamic therapy group (relative risk, 0.94 [95.1% CI, 0.83-1.08]; P = .38). There were no between-group differences for the incidence of the individual components of the primary outcome within the first 7 postoperative days.

Conclusions and relevance

Among high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery, individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy targeting the patient's preoperative resting cardiac index did not reduce the incidence of a composite outcome of acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within the first 7 postoperative days compared with routine hemodynamic therapy.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05648279.
title: Individualized Cardiac Index-Guided Hemodynamic Therapy in High-Risk Patients Undergoing Elective Major Abdominal Surgery: The PELICAN Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Importance

Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a major cause of heart failure that disproportionately affects individuals of predominantly African ancestry, among whom familial clustering of disease is more pronounced relative to those of predominantly European ancestry. Truncating variants in TTN, which encodes the sarcomeric protein titin, are the most common established monogenic cause of DCM. A common CD36 nonsense variant enriched among individuals of African ancestry has also been shown to account for a substantial burden of DCM.

Objective

To compare the contribution of a CD36 nonsense variant to DCM risk with that of truncating variants in TTN and pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other established genes for DCM.

Design, setting, and participants

Multicohort genetic association study including participants of African and European ancestry with exome or genome sequence data and DCM case status from the following 4 US datasets: All of Us Research Program (recruitment: 2017-present; last follow-up: August 27, 2024), Million Veteran Program (recruitment: 2011-present; last follow-up: September 30, 2024), Penn Medicine Biobank (recruitment: 2013-present; last follow-up: November 14, 2022), and the DCM Precision Medicine Study (recruitment: 2016-2020; last follow-up: March 15, 2020).

Exposure

Carrier status for TTN truncating variants, pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 11 high-confidence genes for DCM, and the nonsense variant CD36 Y325* (0, 1, or 2 copies).

Main outcomes and measures

Risk of DCM, prevalence of variant carriers among DCM cases, and population attributable fraction of DCM.

Results

Among 82 623 individuals of predominantly African ancestry across 4 cohorts, the mean age was 53.4 years (SD, 13.9 years), 47 124 were male, and 1316 had DCM. Individuals who were homozygous for the CD36 Y325* risk allele had a higher risk of DCM (odds ratio [OR], 4.8; 95% CI, 3.1-7.3) as did those who were heterozygous (OR, 1.4; 95% CI, 1.2-1.7). TTN truncating variants also conferred an elevated risk of DCM in participants of African ancestry (OR, 8.5; 95% CI, 5.5-13.0). Among 1316 individuals of African ancestry classified as DCM cases, 33 (2.5%) were homozygous for CD36, 56 (4.3%) had TTN truncating variants, and 16 (1.2%) had pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other high-confidence genes for DCM. In population-level analyses incorporating both heterozygous and homozygous CD36 Y325* carriers, the population attributable fraction for CD36 (9.0% [6.2% for heterozygous carriers and 2.8% for homozygous carriers]) surpassed the population attributable fraction for TTN truncating variants (3.7%).

Conclusions and relevance

In 4 US cohorts, an ancestry-specific CD36 variant contributed more to DCM burden among individuals of African ancestry than established genes for DCM, including TTN truncating variants that are typically considered the most common genetic cause. These findings reshape the known genetic architecture of DCM in individuals of African ancestry and highlight the importance of representation in genomic research.
title: A Common CD36 Variant and the Genetic Landscape of Dilated Cardiomyopathy in Individuals of African Ancestry.

summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to quantify psychological constructs from natural language, yet their outputs are typically evaluated only as predictions of an external label. When that label is itself imperfect, optimizing prediction conflates label agreement with construct measurement. No study has applied a multidomain measurement-oriented evaluation to LLM-derived psychological outputs. Objective: We applied 5 psychometric evaluation domains to LLM-derived outputs to test whether measurement-oriented evaluation surfaces properties that prediction-oriented evaluation does not: extraction repeatability, convergent validity with a lexicon-based tool, ecological concurrent validity decomposed into within-person and between-person components, incremental value in a 4-arm comparison with that tool, and method-blinded expert evaluation with structured error attribution. Methods: Thirteen linguistic features were extracted by GPT-5.2 (OpenAI) from 3556 person-days of daily voice narratives collected from 279 call center workers over 15 days via ecological momentary assessment. Features were evaluated across the 5 domains, with Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count, version 22, as the lexicon-based comparator. Multimodel robustness was assessed by re-extracting all features with Google Gemini 2.5 Flash. Results: Features showed high repeatability (mean intraclass correlation coefficient=0.987), construct-dependent convergent validity (Spearman ρ=0.08 to 0.79), and within-person tracking of same-day stress (negative emotion β=0.68). In a 4-arm comparison (baseline, baseline plus lexicon features, baseline plus LLM-derived features, and baseline plus both), LLM features increased explained variance in daily stress from 13.2% to 30.4%, versus 16.9% for the lexicon-based comparator. Among transcripts sampled for maximal method discordance, experts preferred LLM-derived profiles in 83.7% (261/312) of blinded decisions. Error analysis showed that 53% (35/66) of false-positive attributions reflected reference-label limitations, not model failures. Re-extraction with Google Gemini 2.5 Flash replicated key properties (person-level =0.94). Three phenomena were visible under measurement-oriented evaluation that prediction-oriented evaluation does not typically examine: divergence between within-person and between-person effects, reference-label limitations as a dominant error source, and moderation of feature meaning by individual differences. Conclusions: Prediction metrics alone are insufficient for evaluating LLM-derived psychological measures. Measurement-oriented evaluation revealed properties, including level-dependent effects and asymmetric error attribution, that have direct implications for how LLM-based assessment studies interpret their results. For clinical use, the measure is a complement to existing screening instruments for longitudinal monitoring, not a stand-alone diagnostic.
title: Evaluating Large Language Model–Derived Outputs as Psychological Measures: A Five-Domain Psychometric Framework With Application to Daily Stress

summary: Background: AI has increasingly been used to generate synthetic images to overcome the scarcity of large, regulatory-compliant medical image datasets. However, their quality and actual utility for algorithm development across deep learning architectures, medical settings, and image types have been poorly assessed. Objective: This study aimed to review the use of synthetic images for algorithm development and to assess their quality and effects on downstream algorithms trained on these images, according to AI architecture, medical setting, and image type. Methods: The authors conducted a systematic review of studies published between January 2020 and September 2025. PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Embase were searched for peer-reviewed studies evaluating synthetic images generated from human medical imaging data. Data were extracted for imaging modalities, generative architectures, image-quality assessment methods, downstream model performance, explainability approaches, reproducibility practices, and risk of bias. Given substantial heterogeneity and incomplete statistical reporting, findings were synthesized descriptively. Results: A total of 160 studies were included. Generative adversarial network–based architectures dominated image generation (119 studies, 74.4%), although hybrid and diffusion-based approaches became increasingly represented in recent years. Image-quality evaluation was highly heterogeneous: 50 studies included human-reader evidence, and 101 reported an automated image-quality assessment. Synthetic-only training generally underperformed real-data training, including a median Dice similarity coefficient change of –10.2% for segmentation. Adding synthetic data to real training sets was associated with median improvements in classification precision (+7.8%), recall (+5.3%), -score (+5.5%), accuracy (+4.3%), and area under the curve (+4.0%), while the median Dice coefficient improvement was +1.2%. Explainability evidence was reported in 68 (42.5%) studies and was rarely validated against expert annotations. Reproducibility reporting was inconsistent, and only 38% (60/160) of studies were judged to have low overall risk of bias. Conclusions: Unlike previous reviews restricted to particular diseases, imaging modalities, or generative architectures, this review provides a cross-domain quantitative synthesis of both synthetic-image quality assessment and downstream model performance. Synthetic images currently appear more valuable as a complement to real training data than as a replacement, with modest improvements in classification performance, smaller gains in segmentation, and generally poorer performance with synthetic-only training. Background

Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has been shown to be beneficial in persons with type 1 diabetes and others with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, but its role in the treatment of persons with type 2 diabetes not being treated with insulin has needed further study.

Methods

In a 26-week trial conducted at 22 primary care practices in the United States, we randomly assigned adults with type 2 diabetes who were not using insulin to either CGM or routine care (control). The primary outcome was the glycated hemoglobin level at 26 weeks. Key CGM-measured secondary outcomes were tested hierarchically to control the type I error rate.

Results

A total of 145 participants were assigned to the CGM group, and 138 to the routine-care group. Participants ranged in age from 21 to 84 years. The mean (±SD) glycated hemoglobin level decreased from 8.8±1.3% at baseline to 7.2±1.1% at 26 weeks in the CGM group and from 8.7±1.2% to 8.0±1.4% in the routine-care group (adjusted mean difference, -0.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.1 to -0.6; P<0.001). The mean percentage of time that the CGM-measured glucose level was in the glucose-level range of 70 to 180 mg per deciliter was 21 percentage points higher (95% CI, 16 to 26) with CGM than with routine care (P<0.001). The between-group difference in the percentage of time that the glucose level was below 54 mg per deciliter was -0.17 percentage points (95% CI, -0.27 to -0.11; P<0.001 for noninferiority); the difference in the percentage of time that the glucose level was below 70 mg per deciliter was -0.20 percentage points (95% CI, -0.43 to -0.09; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P = 0.004 for superiority). No severe hypoglycemia events were reported.

Conclusions

Among adults with type 2 diabetes that was not being treated with insulin and was being managed in a primary care setting, the use of CGM led to a greater reduction in the glycated hemoglobin level and to a lower risk of hyperglycemia than routine care. Background

The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain.

Methods

In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90.

Results

The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group.

Conclusions

Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. (Funded by the French Ministry of Health; ICRAKI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06032884.).

Importance

The optimal vasopressor dose at which to initiate a second vasopressor in patients with septic shock is uncertain.

Objective

To compare the effects of hospital-level strategies initiating vasopressin infusion at a lower threshold vs a higher threshold on outcomes in patients with septic shock.

Design, setting, and participants

Cluster-randomized, cluster-crossover, pragmatic clinical strategy trial including adult patients receiving vasopressors for septic shock at 13 hospitals in Idaho and Utah from February 1, 2024, to July 31, 2025. The last day of follow-up for the primary outcome was February 17, 2026.

Intervention

Hospital-level implementation of septic shock management strategies recommending fixed-dose vasopressin initiation when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.1 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (lower-threshold strategy) or when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.4 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (higher-threshold strategy). Hospitals were randomized for the first month to an initial strategy (6 hospitals to the lower threshold vs 7 hospitals to the higher threshold) and then crossed over to the alternate strategy monthly thereafter.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome of 28-day mortality and the key secondary outcome of kidney replacement therapy-free days through day 28 were analyzed using multivariable generalized linear mixed-effects models, accounting for trial site and baseline patient characteristics.

Results

There were 3959 unique patients with septic shock (median age, 68 [IQR, 57 to 77] years; 1903 [48%] were female). Of the patients more likely to experience differential management under the tested hospital-level vasopressin dose strategies (maximum vasopressor dose ≥0.07 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent), 1034 of 1521 (68.0%) cared for under the lower-threshold strategy received vasopressin compared with 651 of 1526 (42.7%) cared for under the higher-threshold strategy. In the hospital-level strategy recommending a lower-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation, the maximum vasopressor dose received prior to vasopressin initiation was a median of 0.14 (IQR, 0.10 to 0.22) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent vs 0.34 (IQR, 0.16 to 0.42) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent in the hospital-level strategy recommending a higher-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation. Mortality at 28 days occurred in 628 of 1975 patients (31.8%) treated with the hospital-level strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower-dose threshold of other vasopressors vs 655 of 1984 patients (33.0%) treated with the higher-threshold strategy (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87 to 1.06], P = .62; adjusted risk difference, -0.4 [95% CI, -2.7 to 1.3] percentage points). Patients in both strategies for vasopressin initiation had a median of 29 (IQR, -1 to 29) kidney replacement therapy-free days (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.91 to 1.14]).

Conclusions and relevance

In this large, pragmatic clinical trial comparing the effectiveness of 2 hospital-level strategies for second-line vasopressor management in septic shock, a strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower dose of other vasopressors did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with a strategy recommending vasopressin initiation at a higher dose of other vasopressors.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06217562.
title: Effect of Vasopressin Initiation Threshold on Septic Shock Mortality: The VASSPR Cluster Crossover Randomized Strategy Trial.

Importance

International guidelines recommend dobutamine for management of septic shock and cardiac dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion in adults based on very low-certainty evidence. Randomized trials are lacking on the effect of intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine on postoperative outcomes in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control.

Objective

To determine whether intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduces acute kidney injury (AKI) within 7 postoperative days in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control.

Design, setting, and participants

This randomized, open-label clinical trial in 39 tertiary hospitals in China enrolled adults with septic shock who were undergoing surgical source control between June 2024 and August 2025. Follow-up ended on November 15, 2025.

Intervention

Intraoperative, intravenous infusion of dobutamine (up to 5 µg/kg/min) combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine alone.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was new-onset AKI or worsening of preoperative AKI within 7 days after surgery, defined using Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. The 11 secondary outcomes included Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score on postoperative day 1 and urine output 1 hour post intervention.

Results

Among 584 patients (median [IQR] age, 67.5 [55.0-76.0] years; 192 [32.9%] females), new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days occurred in 22.8% (66/290) randomized to receive dobutamine plus norepinephrine vs 34.7% (102/294) randomized to receive norepinephrine alone (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 0.64 [95% CI, 0.49-0.83]). No significant differences were observed in 9 of the 11 secondary outcomes. SOFA scores on postoperative day 1 (adjusted difference, -0.53 [95% CI, -0.98 to -0.07]) were lower and urine output 1 hour post intervention (adjusted difference, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.03 to 1.07] mL/kg/h) was higher in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group. Stage 2 and 3 AKI were lower in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group compared with the norepinephrine alone group (stage 2: 4.8% vs 9.9%; ARR, 0.48 [95% CI, 0.26-0.88]; stage 3: 7.9% vs 13.6%; ARR, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.35-0.91]). Tachycardia (heart rate >100/min) occurred more frequently in patients receiving dobutamine and norepinephrine than norepinephrine alone.

Conclusions and relevance

Among adult patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control, intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduced the incidence of new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days compared with norepinephrine.

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06462313.

summary:
Importance

Fluid therapy is ubiquitous in the intensive care unit (ICU) but carries risks, especially in mechanically ventilated patients. Contemporary global practice across dose, indication, and type is unknown.

Objective

To characterize ICU fluid practices in mechanically ventilated adults.

Design, setting, and participants

International prospective observational cohort study between April 2024 and July 2025, across 206 ICUs in 41 countries on 6 continents. Consecutive adult patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation within 3 days of ICU admission and ventilated 24 hours or more. Exclusion criteria were age younger than 16 years and transfer under mechanical ventilation from another ICU.

Exposures

Fluid volume, indication, and type after intubation.

Main outcomes and measures

Key measures included (1) total infused volume and daily fluid balance over 7 days after intubation; (2) the indication for fluid therapy over the first 3 days after intubation; (3) the proportion of total administered fluid volume attributable to each fluid type over the first 3 days after intubation.

Results

Among 2454 patients analyzed (median age, 63 years [IQR, 49-73 years]; 63.6% [1560] male), median daily fluid input peaked on day 1 at 3.0 L (IQR, 2.2-4.0 L) and declined to 2.6 L (IQR, 1.8-3.5 L) through day 6. Daily fluid balance (median, 0.9 L; IQR, 0.1-1.9 L on day 1) decreased to less than 0.3 L (IQR, -0.5 to 1.2 L) by day 3 and remained near-neutral through day 6. Maintenance and replacement fluids (to meet daily requirements and to correct ongoing losses; 31.9%) and creep fluids (to deliver medications and maintain catheter patency; 30.9%) were the primary indications, whereas resuscitation (to restore circulating blood volume; 16.0%) accounted for a smaller proportion. Isotonic balanced crystalloids (48.9%) and isotonic saline (0.9% sodium chloride) (27.0%) were common; colloids were rare (1.3%). Substantial between-site variation persisted after adjustment for case-mix.

Conclusions and relevance

In this prospective international cohort study, fluid therapy varied widely among mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, with maintenance and creep fluids-rather than resuscitation fluids-accounting for most total volume.

Objective

To characterise the reporting completeness of clinical trials involving large language model (LLM) interventions using established reporting guidelines.

Design

Systematic review and meta-research analysis.

Data sources

Bibliographic databases (Embase, Medline, and CENTRAL) were searched for trial reports and protocols, and trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were searched for trial registrations published from 1 January 2017 to 6 December 2025.

Eligibility criteria

Trial reports, trial protocols, and trial registrations describing clinical trials of LLM interventions in medicine. LLM interventions used for a healthcare function in a clinical trial setting included patient education, clinical documentation, communication support, triage, care navigation, management recommendations, or clinical decision support. Eligible studies prospectively assigned human participants to the intervention and evaluated a health related biomedical or behavioural outcome.

Main outcome measures

Overall study level and item level reporting completeness assessed using reporting guidelines matched to study design and purpose, including TRIPOD-LLM (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis-LLM), CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2025 and CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 and SPIRIT-AI, CHART (Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool), and the WHO Trial Registration Dataset (version 1.3.1). Two reviewers independently screened and extracted trial and intervention characteristics, and three calibrated raters assessed item level reporting completeness.

Results

The systematic search yielded 461 records, including 68 trial reports, 15 protocols, and 378 registrations. Trial reports were predominantly small sample, single site randomised studies published between 2024 and 2025, spanning diverse clinical specialties and primarily targeting patient facing education and management recommendations. Mean reporting completeness was modest across eligible trial reports (TRIPOD-LLM 40%, CONSORT 2025 44%, CONSORT-AI 59%, CHART 52%), trial protocols (SPIRIT 2025 51%, SPIRIT-AI 57%), and trial registrations (WHO Trial Registration Dataset 61%). Clinical trial reports of LLM interventions prioritise narrative framing and commentary over the methodological detail needed for replication, risk-of-bias assessment, and governance of model performance over time. Critical methodological elements for reproducibility, including data and intervention provenance, input preprocessing, model versioning and access modality, inference parameters, output postprocessing, as well as protocol, data, and code access, were inconsistently reported. Harms planning, monitoring, and reporting were often incompletely reported, limiting the critical appraisal of the safety of LLM interventions in healthcare.

Conclusion

Clinical trials of LLM interventions show modest adherence to established reporting guidelines, with persistent underreporting of LLM specific methodological details, reproducibility artefacts (protocols, data, code), and harms reporting required to support reproducibility and confident appraisal of safety risks before their clinical translation.

summary:
Background

Existing data on malformations associated with benzodiazepine use in pregnancy are conflicting.

Objective

To assess the risk for major congenital malformations from first-trimester exposure to benzodiazepines.

Design

Population-based U.S. cohort study.

Setting

Medicaid (2000-2018) and Merative MarketScan (2003-2020) databases.

Participants

Pregnant persons enrolled from 90 days before pregnancy to 30 days after delivery, and their live-born infants enrolled for 90 days after birth.

Measurements

Exposure was defined as at least 1 fill of a benzodiazepine in the first trimester. Primary outcomes were any major congenital malformation and organ-specific malformations previously associated with benzodiazepine exposure. The investigators estimated relative risks (RRs) comparing exposed versus unexposed pregnancies with propensity score fine stratification weights to control for confounders. An RR of 1.3 or higher was prespecified as clinically significant.

Results

In total, 51 339 of 2 478 434 (2.1%) publicly insured and 27 779 of 1 750 721 (1.6%) commercially insured pregnancies had benzodiazepine exposure. The adjusted absolute risks for any malformation in exposed versus unexposed pregnancies were 4.0% versus 4.1% for Medicaid and 4.9% versus 4.8% for MarketScan. The pooled adjusted RR was 0.99 (95% CI, 0.96 to 1.03). Associations with organ-specific malformations were not consistently observed in sensitivity analyses, nor was a dose-response relationship observed. Analyses of different benzodiazepines yielded similar results. The risk for selected organ-specific malformations was increased in some analyses of coexposure to benzodiazepines and other psychoactive medications, but a consistent pattern did not emerge.

Limitations

Potential nondifferential exposure and outcome misclassification; analyses restricted to malformations prevalent at birth.

Conclusion

No substantial increase in the risk for malformations was consistently identified across data sources. Findings from coexposure analyses were inconsistent and warrant further study.

Primary funding source

National Institute of Child Health and Human Development.
title: Benzodiazepine Use Early in Pregnancy and Risk for Congenital Malformations.

summary:
Importance

One in 5 heart transplant candidates in the US die or are delisted without transplant. Donor hearts are currently allocated by a 6-status therapy-based system criticized for limited risk stratification and susceptibility to gaming.

Objective

To develop a new heart allocation policy based on an objective medical urgency score that ranks candidates based on the interaction between physiology and mechanical circulatory support.

Design, setting, and participants

Registry-based observational study using data from the US organ transplant system. All adult (aged ≥18 years) heart transplant candidates from January 2019 to August 2025 were included, split into training (2019-2023), validation (2023-2024), and test (2024-2025) datasets.

Main outcomes and measures

A marginal structural model of 6-week mortality without transplant was estimated (the US Candidate Risk Score [US-CRS]). Eight models were compared in held-out data by weighted time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and calibration by status. Finally, US-CRS was converted into an allocation policy and a match-run simulation of waitlist reordering was performed compared with the current 6-status system.

Results

Adult heart transplant candidates were partitioned into consecutive training (n = 21 859), validation (n = 7897), and test (n = 8256) datasets (mean [SD] age, 53 [13] years; 74% male). The chosen US-CRS model included 5 laboratory values and 4 therapeutic devices (durable left ventricular assist device, intra-aortic balloon pump, microaxial flow pump, and advanced mechanical circulatory support). In test-set cross-sections of candidates actively waiting on the same calendar date, US-CRS had similar or significantly higher time-dependent AUC than the current 6-status system (mean AUC, 0.807 vs 0.693, respectively) and acceptable calibration by status, especially for candidates who received their status by exception. In match-run analysis (n = 45 530 donor hearts), a US-CRS-based system led to 67% of transplant recipients moving down in rank order and increased observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality for the first candidate on the match run from 11.2% (95% CI, 10.1%-12.5%) under the current system to 15.7% (95% CI, 13.9%-17.6%) under the US-CRS-based system.

Conclusions and relevance

In this registry-based study of US heart transplant candidates, a US-CRS-based allocation system prioritized sicker candidates with higher mortality without transplant compared with the current medical urgency statuses.
title: Development and Validation of an Adult Medical Urgency Score for US Donor Heart Allocation.

Background

In hereditary angioedema, a rare bradykinin-mediated condition, oral on-demand treatments facilitating prompt administration and providing rapid, sustained relief and attack resolution remain scant. We investigated the efficacy and safety of deucrictibant, an oral bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist, for on-demand treatment of hereditary angioedema attacks.

Methods

RAPIDe-3 was a phase 3, double-blind, 2 × 2 crossover trial in adolescent and adult participants (aged ≥12 to <18 years and aged ≥18 to ≤75 years, respectively) with hereditary angioedema, at 59 sites across 24 countries on six continents. Eligible participants had hereditary angioedema, including those with normal C1 inhibitor associated with a documented genetic variant, at least two attacks within the last 3 months before screening, and experience with effectively using conventional on-demand therapies for hereditary angioedema attacks. Participants were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to one of two double-blind crossover sequences to treat two attacks with a 20 mg oral deucrictibant immediate-release capsule or placebo as either deucrictibant-placebo or placebo-deucrictibant, stratified by age and use of long-term prophylaxis. The primary endpoint was time to onset of symptom relief, defined as Patient Global Impression of Change rating of at least a little better. Safety was assessed in all participants who received any dose of study drug. RAPIDe-3 is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06343779) and is complete.

Findings

Between April 4, 2024, and Sept 1, 2025, 149 people were assessed for eligibility, and 134 eligible participants (ten [7%] adolescents and 124 [93%] adults) were randomly allocated. 58 (43%) were male and 76 (57%) were female, and the median age was 38·0 years (IQR 27·0-50·0). 113 participants treated 201 attacks. The primary efficacy analysis included 88 participants with paired treated attacks. Of these, 47 (53%) participants were female and 41 (47%) were male, and 60 (68%), 16 (18%), 4 (5%), and 1 (1%) were White, Asian, Black, and American Indian or Alaska Native, respectively. Onset of symptom relief occurred significantly faster with deucrictibant than placebo, with median times of 1·28 h (95% CI 1·05 to 1·52) and more than 12 h (5·82 to >12), respectively (p<0·0001). Fatigue was the only adverse event reported more than once within 3 days post-treatment: a single event was reported by two participants, one of which was deemed unrelated to treatment. Across the study, no treatment-related adverse events were assessed as severe or serious, and no adverse events led to treatment discontinuation.

Interpretation

Oral deucrictibant provided faster times to symptom relief than placebo and was generally well tolerated. These results support the use of deucrictibant as potentially the first orally administered bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist for the treatment of attacks of bradykinin-mediated angioedema, including hereditary angioedema, and may address an unmet need for options that are effective and well tolerated, with convenient administration.

Pharvaris.

summary:
Importance

Nicotinamide riboside, a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide precursor, has been proposed as a potential disease-modifying therapy for Parkinson disease based on preclinical and early studies. Whether prolonged oral nicotinamide riboside improves clinical outcomes in Parkinson disease is unknown.

Objective

To determine whether nicotinamide riboside improves clinical outcomes in Parkinson disease compared with placebo.

Design, setting, and participants

Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 clinical trial conducted at 11 centers in Norway. Eligible participants were patients aged 35 years or older with Parkinson disease diagnosed within 2 years before enrollment, Hoehn and Yahr disease stage less than 3, abnormal dopamine transporter scintigraphy findings confirming dopaminergic nigrostriatal denervation, and stable dopaminergic treatment before enrollment. Of 537 screened individuals, 410 were randomized from May 6, 2020, to June 20, 2024, and 393 were included in the primary analysis. Final follow-up was completed on June 19, 2025.

Interventions

Patients were randomized to receive oral nicotinamide riboside, 500 mg twice daily (n = 206), or matching placebo (n = 204) for 52 weeks.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was change from baseline to week 52 in the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale total score (MDS-UPDRS parts I-III; range, 0-236, with higher scores indicating more severe disease; clinically important differences for improvement and worsening, 6.7 and 5.2 points, respectively), analyzed using a mixed model for repeated measures. The 5 key secondary outcomes were the individual parts I, II, and III of the MDS-UPDRS; dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography brain imaging findings; and the Non-Motor Symptoms Scale score (NMSS; range, 0-360, with higher scores indicating greater nonmotor symptom burden).

Results

Among the 393 participants in the primary analysis, the mean age was 65.6 (SD, 9.4) years and 133 (34%) were female. At week 52, the total MDS-UPDRS score increased by 2.45 (95% CI, 0.80-4.10) points with nicotinamide riboside and decreased by 0.27 (95% CI, -1.95 to 1.40) points with placebo, yielding an adjusted mean difference of 2.72 points (95% CI, 0.47-4.98 points; P = .02), favoring placebo. Of the 5 prespecified key secondary outcomes, 4 showed no significant difference, but nonmotor symptom burden worsened more with nicotinamide riboside (NMSS score adjusted mean difference, 4.22 [95% CI, 1.07-7.37] points; P = .009). Serious adverse events occurred in 17 (8.3%) of 205 participants receiving nicotinamide riboside and 29 (14.1%) of 205 receiving placebo in the safety population.

Conclusions and relevance

Among patients with early Parkinson disease, nicotinamide riboside treatment for 52 weeks did not improve clinical outcomes and was associated with worse clinical outcomes than placebo. These findings do not support nicotinamide riboside as a disease-modifying treatment for Parkinson disease.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03568968.
title: Nicotinamide Riboside for Patients With Early-Stage Parkinson Disease: The NOPARK Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Objective

To evaluate the association between quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy and subsequent risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Design

Nationwide, population based matched case-control study.

Setting

Population of Sweden, from 1 January 2006 to 31 December 2023.

Participants

624 713 singleton births among nulliparous women aged 16-35 years in Sweden between 2006 and 2023; 92 620 (14.8%) women had received quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy.

Main outcome measures

Risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes associated with quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination, with preterm birth (<37 weeks), including its subtypes, and spontaneous preterm birth as primary outcomes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, prelabour rupture of membranes, small for gestational age infant (<10th centile), severe small for gestational age infant (<3rd centile), stillbirth, and neonatal mortality as secondary outcomes. Effect modification by age at human papillomavirus vaccination was assessed. Conditional logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios and adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Results

After adjustment for confounders, quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination was associated with lower odds of all included adverse pregnancy outcomes. Statistically significant associations were observed for preterm birth (<37 weeks) (adjusted odds ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.91 to 0.99), very preterm birth (28 weeks to 31 weeks) (0.85, 0.75 to 0.97), spontaneous preterm birth (0.95, 0.91 to 0.99), preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (0.93, 0.87 to 1.00), and severe small for gestational age infant (0.92, 0.87 to 0.97). Risk reduction was generally more pronounced among women vaccinated at younger ages.

Conclusions

Quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy was associated with a lower risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes, particularly among women vaccinated at earlier ages, extending benefits of human papillomavirus vaccination beyond cancer prevention.

summary: Transparency in Coverage Final Rules (CMS 9882-F) Introduction Consistent with the President’s Executive Order 14221 , “Making America Healthy Again by Empowering Patients with Clear, Accurate, and Actionable Healthcare Pricing Information,” on October 5, 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services (through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services), in partnership with the Departments of Labor and the Department of the Treasury (collectively, the Departments) jointly finalized changes to the Transparency in Coverage regulations to improve the accessibility of pricing disclosures to participants, beneficiaries, and enrollees, and the standardization and reliability of the public pricing disclosures from non-grandfathered group health plans and health insurance issuers offering non-grandfathered group or individual health insurance coverage. These changes build on the historic disclosure requirements the Departments issued in the Transparency in Coverage final rules on Nov. 12, 2020 (the 2020 final rules) in line with the President’s June 24, 2019, Executive Order (EO) 13877, “Improving Price and Quality Transparency in American Healthcare to Put Patients First” and EO 14221, “Making America Healthy Again by Empowering Patients with Clear, Accurate, and Actionable Healthcare Pricing Information.” This fact sheet discusses the provisions of the Transparency in Coverage final rules (CMS-9882-F) that amend the 2020 final rules. You can access the final rules in the Federal Register at: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/2026-20447/transparency-in-coverage Under the 2020 final rules, non-grandfathered group health plans and health insurance issuers offering non-grandfathered group or individual health insurance coverage are required to post machine-readable files monthly for each plan or coverage they offer — an in-network rate file disclosing in-network rates for all covered items and services, an allowed amount file disclosing out-of-network allowed amounts and the associated billed charges for covered items and services, and a prescription drug file disclosing in-network rates and historical net prices for covered prescription drugs. These requirements became applicable in July 2022. 1 Improved Standardization, Accuracy, and Accessibility of the In-Network Rate and Out-of-Network Allowed Amount Machine-Readable Files Based on internal assessment and external stakeholder feedback received since implementation began, the Departments have identified three main barriers to fully achieving the goals of the 2020 final rules: inaccessibility due to the large size of the machine-readable files, data ambiguity due to lack of contextual information alongside the raw data, and areas of misalignment with the Hospital Price Transparency rule that make comparing data across disclosures challenging. Reducing the Number and Size of Machine-Readable Files and Increasing Accessibility to Make Data More Meaningful A major driver of large in-network rate file sizes involves including provider-negotiated rates for items or services the provider is unlikely to furnish because of their specialty and the nature of the item or service (e.g., rates for podiatrists to perform heart surgery). This occurs because payer-provider contracts often negotiate rates at the provider organization level for every provider who is a member of the organization, regardless of clinical specialty. To address these unlikely provider-rate combinations, the final rules include amendments to: Require group health plans and health insurance issuers to exclude from their In-network Rate Files provider-rate combinations for items and services that providers would be unlikely to be reimbursed for given that provider’s specialty area. The provision requires plans and issuers to determine which provider-rate combinations to exclude by using their internal provider taxonomies or other internal rules used during the claims adjudication process to determine if the provider should be reimbursed for the item or service given that provider's specialty; Post the internal provider taxonomy mapping or other rules they used to prepare each In-network Rate File in a new file called the Taxonomy File; and Post a new file called a Utilization File for each In-network Rate File, which will include all providers who have submitted and received reimbursement for at least one claim for a covered item or service for the most recent plan or policy year ending six months before the posting of the file. To reduce duplicative data, the Departments finalized a change to the level at which group health plans and health insurance issuers must report data in the In-network Rate File. Under this provision, plans and issuers must prepare one In-network Rate File for each provider network they maintain or contract with, rather than for each plan or policy they offer, as required by the 2020 final rules. Because it is very common for multiple plans offered by the same issuer or administered by the same service provider to leverage the same provider networks with the same negotiated rates, requiring network-level reporting will streamline how rates are reported, reducing both the number and the size of In-network Rate Files. Further, reporting in-network rates at the network level also aligns with how the Hospital Price Transparency data is typically reported. Aligning payer and hospital data reporting will help normalize data across different systems, improve consistency, and make comparisons between the payer and hospital machine-readable files easier for file users. Improving Data Availability The Departments have received feedback and observed that many group health plans and health insurance issuers include limited or no data in their Out-of-network Allowed Amount Files, which may be due, in part, to the current 20-claims threshold for reporting. This has limited the transparency of out-of-network pricing information to the public and, in turn, limited what researchers, academics, and developers can analyze. The Departments include three amendments for the Out-of-network Allowed Amount Files to address insufficient data: 1) require payers to aggregate their Allowed Amount Files by insurance market type (large group, small group, individual, and self-insured); 2) lower the claims threshold for reporting payment of out-of-network allowed amounts from 20 to 11 claims; and 3) increase the amount of out-of-network data disclosed to the public to better position researchers and academics to conduct analyses to inform the public. Taken together, the Departments expect these amendments will significantly increase the amount of out-of-network data disclosed to the public. The barrier to meeting the 11-claim threshold will be lower, particularly when data is aggregated by market type and the reporting period is more than twice as long. Further, the Departments understand from stakeholder feedback that out-of-network allowed amounts across plans and policies are most aligned by market type. Providing this data at the market-type level will allow users to compare allowed amounts for plans within the same market, which, based on feedback, the Departments anticipate will better position researchers and academics to conduct analyses to inform the public. The final rules also require additional data elements to provide context around the reported data. Group health plans and health insurance issuers will be required to report the plan’s or policy’s product type (e.g., HMO, PPO) for each plan or policy represented in an In-network Rate File and Out-of-network Allowed Amount File, as well as the common provider network name and network identifier associated with the provider network represented in the In-network Rate File. Making Data Easier to Locate The final rules include two provisions to help users locate the machine-readable files. First, plans and issuers will be required to publish a plain text file (.txt file) located in the root folder of the plan’s or issuer’s website (or under certain circumstances, for another party to publish the file on its public website on the plan’s or issuer’s behalf) with information on the specific location of the machine-readable files. This file must also include contact information, including a monitored email address for an individual or group dedicated to receiving and responding to inquiries and issues related to the machine-readable files. In addition, plans and issuers will be required to add a link in the footer of the homepage of their website titled “Price Transparency” or “Transparency in Coverage” that routes directly to the publicly available web page that hosts the machine-readable files. This will allow for a standardized and predictable navigation path for users trying to find the files. Together, these requirements will help automate locating and downloading the machine-readable files and provide a point of contact for questions about or clarification on the data within the files. These requirements will also apply to the prescription drug machine-readable file. These provisions align with current requirements under the Hospital Price Transparency rules. Reducing Stakeholder Burden Beginning in the second year of implementation and continuing thereafter, these final rules are expected to generate a net cost savings to plans and issuers of approximately $174.5 million annually, due in part to the reduced reporting cadence for certain machine-readable files. The Departments are requiring plans and issuers to update and post the In-network Rate and Out-of-network Allowed Amount Files quarterly rather than monthly to help lower data storage and hosting costs, decrease bandwidth needs, and reduce ongoing maintenance expenses. Plans, issuers, and researchers have indicated that, since provider networks and rates do not change significantly from month to month, switching to a quarterly reporting cadence will not lead to a significant reduction in meaningful data. This reduced reporting cadence will also provide more time for file users to analyze the data, as some file users have informed the Departments that they have difficulty keeping up with the pace of downloading and ingesting the file data monthly. This change in reporting cadence along with the reduction of both the size and number of machine-readable files will reduce the current burden associated with preparing, ingesting, analyzing, and storing the public disclosures. To promote standardization across payers’ files and remain consistent with current industry practice, the final rules require plans and issuers to use a single format. The Departments intend to specify the JSON format in guidance for all machine-readable files other than the text file, which is required to be published as a plain text (.txt) file. summary: Background: Conversational AI systems are increasingly being deployed in health care for clinical decision support, but their performance varies substantially across patient communication styles, health literacy levels, and behavioral patterns. Static benchmarks cannot capture multiturn dynamics through which this variation compounds, and no current evaluation framework implements structured AI risk management guidance for conversational health care AI. The result is a structural risk: AI systems may perform well in aggregate while failing disproportionately for the populations they are intended to help. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate a patient simulation framework that aligns with the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) Map and Measure functions, providing an empirical basis for identifying and characterizing performance risks in conversational clinical AI across medical, linguistic, and behavioral patient variations. We applied the framework to a conversational decision aid for antidepressant selection in major depressive disorder (the AI decision aid). Methods: The simulator integrated three profile dimensions: (1) medical profiles constructed from All of Us electronic health records using risk ratio gating; (2) linguistic profiles modeling a health literacy gradient and condition-specific communication; and (3) behavioral profiles representing cooperative, distracted, and adversarial engagement. We generated 500 simulated conversations and evaluated profile fidelity through human annotation and a large language model (LLM) judge, and then assessed downstream effects on the AI decision aid’s concept retrieval and antidepressant recommendations. Results: The patient simulator expressed medical concepts with high fidelity (96.6% accuracy across 8210 concepts), with substantial human interannotator agreement (κ=0.73) and LLM-judge agreement against human annotators (κ=0.78). Behavioral profiles were reliably distinguished (κ=0.93; near perfect agreement), and linguistic profiles showed substantial agreement at the lower bound of the substantial range (κ=0.61), which can be considered adequate to support profile-level analysis. The framework revealed monotonic degradation in AI decision aid performance across the health literacy gradient. Rank-1 concept retrieval increased from 47.6% for limited health literacy to 81.9% for proficient health literacy, with corresponding declines in antidepressant recommendation accuracy. Conclusions: Patient simulation grounded in the NIST AI RMF exposes measurable performance risks in conversational health care AI that static benchmarks miss, with direct equity implications. Health literacy operates as a structural risk factor, with degraded performance concentrated in patients carrying the greatest burden of psychiatric illness. The framework supports targeted risk-mitigation interventions before deployment. While we evaluated the framework only on antidepressant selection, extending it to other clinical decision-aid tasks remains an assignment for future work.
title: A Patient Simulation Framework for Risk Assessment of Conversational Health Care AI: Development and Evaluation Study

summary: Shapley value explanations are increasingly used to provide added transparency for “black-box” prediction models in healthcare. summary: AI-oncology evidence is expanding too quickly for static manual surveillance. summary: Despite advances in brain biomarkers using neural networks, the effects of body mass on brain structure have been neglected, particularly in connection with noncommunicable diseases. summary: Healthcare workers (HCWs) face elevated risk for burnout and stress-related disorders, yet conventional self-report assessments are limited by professional stigma and underreporting. summary: Although large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for discharge summary generation, their performance in longer hospitalizations remains less well studied. summary: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome is associated with a high risk of mortality, yet accurate individual risk prediction remains limited. summary: Urine biomarkers promise to improve noninvasive detection and molecular characterization of genitourinary malignancies. summary: Background: Social media platforms, particularly YouTube (Google LLC), are important sources of health information, but also significant vectors for misinformation and pseudoscience. While many studies analyze the content and sentiment of this information, the dynamic, sequential nature of user interactions, which can shape belief formation and community dynamics, remains poorly understood. Objective: This study aimed to explore the applicability of network analysis and process mining techniques for identifying and comparing structural and emotional patterns of conversational flow within a retrieved corpus of YouTube comments from videos about scientific or pseudoscientific health treatments. Methods: We conducted an exploratory observational study using publicly available YouTube comment threads posted between 2011 and 2025 from videos categorized as either “scientific” (20,387 comments) or “pseudoscientific” (32,025 comments) using an automated pipeline that combined API-based data extraction, large language model–based video classification, and natural language processing techniques for multilingual sentiment and thematic classification of comments. We then applied process mining to model the temporal sequences of interactions, and network analysis to map the relationships between conversational topics. Results: Network analysis revealed divergent conversational cores. In the scientific corpus, negative expressions of feelings and negative comparisons had greater normalized node strength, while medical treatment and advice requests were also relatively more prominent. In the pseudoscientific corpus, positive expressions of feelings, thanking, compliments, and emoji-only or brief acknowledgments showed greater prominence. Process mining showed a more heterogeneous combination of negative, positive, and neutral activities in the scientific corpus, whereas the most frequent pathways in the pseudoscientific corpus were concentrated around positive expressions of feelings, thanking, compliments, and brief messages of acknowledgment, or simply emojis. Conclusions: The application of network analysis and process mining techniques revealed distinct patterns in the conversational dynamics of health-related YouTube discussions. Within the sampled corpora, scientific discussions appeared more compatible with mixed-valence evaluation and treatment-related exchanges, whereas pseudoscientific discussions showed patterns more consistent with interpersonal affirmation and socioemotional bonding. These preliminary findings suggest that network analysis and process mining are promising approaches for investigating online health communication and misinformation ecosystems. They also suggest that public health strategies may benefit from considering the affective and community-bonding dimensions of engagement in misinformation communities alongside information provision.
title: Exploring Conversational Dynamics in Scientific and Pseudoscientific Health Communities on YouTube: Process Mining and Network Analysis Study

summary: Background: Training mental health clinicians to conduct standardized clinical assessments is challenging due to a lack of scalable, realistic practice opportunities. Methods: We implemented a system that used an LLM to simulate patients with specified symptom profiles, demographic backgrounds, and distinct communication styles. The system’s performance was analyzed through a mixed methods evaluation, which included a formal assessment by 5 experienced clinical raters who conducted simulated structured Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) interviews with 4 virtual patient personae, scored them on the scale, and provided qualitative feedback on the system’s clinical plausibility, narrative cohesion, and dialogue realism. summary: Background: Periodontitis is one of the most prevalent yet preventable oral diseases, as indicated by multiple clinical and radiographic factors. As these factors are recorded in electronic health records (EHRs), their reuse offers opportunities for personalized risk assessment and targeted prevention. Predictive AI and traditional machine learning models support fragmented detection tasks but lack the integration of textual and imaging predictors. Emerging multimodal large language models (M-LLMs) show promise in combining these data sources for clinical assessment. Evaluating the capabilities of M-LLMs and comparing them against the current clinical standard are therefore essential to determine their potential as digital assistants. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the ability of M-LLMs to assess periodontitis risk and suggest prevention strategies, based on EHR data and radiographic findings. Each M-LLM was individually evaluated by periodontal experts, benchmarked against other models, and compared with a periodontist as a reference. Methods: A vignette study was conducted following TRIPOD (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis) guidelines for the evaluation of LLMs. Ten periodontal vignettes were created, each including a panoramic radiograph and textual EHR data. Three LLMs capable of reasoning and handling multimodal data were compared to a periodontist who generated outputs manually, based on the same prompts and input data. Periodontal experts rated all outputs across 6 predefined criteria on a 5-point Likert scale. Statistical analyses evaluated overall performance per model and tested whether performance varied per model, scenario complexity, or rater. Results: GPT o1 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4 showed strong performance, with 86.7% and 85.6% of ratings deemed acceptable—comparable to the periodontist’s output (87.8%). Gemini 2.5 Pro was rated significantly lower than both the periodontist and the other models (59.4% acceptable; <.002). Radiographic interpretation consistently received lower scores than other abilities across all models and the periodontist, with Gemini rated below the acceptable threshold. The time required for completion ranged from approximately 10 seconds for Claude to 37 seconds for Gemini; 3 minutes, 22 seconds, for GPT; and 5 minutes, 57 seconds, for the periodontist. Conclusions: M-LLMs demonstrated strong reasoning abilities in periodontal assessment. Across all models, unacceptable elements were consistently related to errors in radiographic interpretation, though refined prompting or newer model versions may improve this. Notably, even when radiographic findings were incorrect and plaque-retentive factors were absent, outputs were still rated well, indicating that EHR data alone provide a substantial basis. For clinical applicability, M-LLMs must at least perform comparably to a periodontist and meet the quality standards set by periodontal experts—a bar that GPT and Claude appear to approach.

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Human-autonomy teaming (HAT) has the potential to reshape surgical practice by fostering true partnership between surgeons and intelligent systems. We identified and analyzed 92 peer-reviewed studies published between 2019 and 2025. The review focused on data modalities (kinematics, video, and biosignals), model architectures, and validation environments. To assess translational maturity, each study was evaluated using the NASA technology readiness level (TRL) scale and mapped to the Yang et al levels of autonomy for surgical robotics, alongside 6 additional dimensions: real-time capability, interpretability, adaptivity, validation environment, external validation, and clinical integration. <strong>Results:</strong> Our analysis of the 92 included studies reveals a dominant shift toward multimodal data integration and deep learning architectures. While high performance is frequently reported on benchmark datasets, significant barriers to HAT integration persist. The TRL analysis shows that 77.2% (71/92) of studies remain at TRL 3 (proof-of-concept), with only 2.2% (2/92) reaching TRL 5 or above. Furthermore, 96.7% (89/92) of studies operate at Yang autonomy level 0, providing no autonomous functionality beyond classification. We identified that 91.3% (84/92) of models are static, with no user-specific adaptation, 38% (35/92) lack any external validation, and validation practices remain inconsistent across the field. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Current AI techniques provide a robust foundation for objective skill assessment, but they are not yet ready for autonomous teaming. title: Machine Learning for Human-Autonomy Teaming in Surgical Skill Assessment: Scoping Review

summary: Neoadjuvant immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are standard of care for resectable stage IIIB–D melanoma, but knowledge gaps remain regarding optimal treatment type, long-term survival, postsurgical management and clinical, histopathological or molecular subgroups.
